name: Medial meniscus posterior root
description: Central attachment of the medial posterior horn to the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia, behind the medial tibial eminence and just in front of the PCL tibial attachment. On coronal images it runs down and centrally from the posterior horn to the tibia just lateral to the medial articular cartilage; on sagittal images near the notch it is the short dark band beside the PCL. It is mostly low signal but often striated, because it is made of several fiber bundles. Coronal T2-weighted or PD fat-sat images show it best, checked against sagittal and axial images.

normal_values.attachment_center: ≈9.6 mm posterior and ≈0.7 mm lateral to the apex of the medial tibial eminence (≈11.5 mm direct), cadaver
normal_values.distance_to_pcl_attachment: ≈8 mm from the nearest margin of the PCL tibial attachment in cadavers (Johannsen 2012), but ≈3 mm (3.3 ± 1.8 mm) on 7 T MRI in volunteers (Marcus 2026); a root lying close to the PCL is normal

variants_pitfalls: The normal root is usually several fiber bundles with mixed, stripe-like signal on fluid-sensitive images, even in asymptomatic young adults (Wang 2018), unlike the uniformly dark medial anterior root. Striation alone is not a tear. Call a tear when fluid-bright signal reaches the root surface with a cleft, irregularity or distortion; a cleft through the full height of the root, or a missing root, is a complete tear, and a partial-height cleft is a partial root tear, not normal striation.

Root tear = radial tear or avulsion within about 9–10 mm of the tibial attachment. Signs: vertical fluid cleft or truncation on coronal T2 images, a 'ghost meniscus' (the meniscus vanishes on one sagittal slice and reappears on the next) and a radial cleft on axial images; in one arthroscopy-correlated series MRI had 86–90% sensitivity and 94–95% specificity, coronal T2 being the most useful sequence (Lee 2008). Partial root tears are subtle and rarely give a ghost sign.

Extrusion of the body by more than 3 mm is the main secondary sign: root tears were present in 42% of knees with >3 mm extrusion versus 3% with ≤3 mm (Costa 2004). A subchondral insufficiency fracture of the medial femoral condyle should send you to the root: medial root or posterior horn radial tears were present in 71% of 253 knees with SIFK, and 91% of those tears had ≥3 mm extrusion (Clark 2024).

A ghost meniscus is not specific to a root tear: it also follows a complete radial tear of the posterior horn and prior meniscectomy or root repair. Check the surgical history and confirm on coronal T2 images that the root is truly discontinuous before reporting a tear.
